items.title: Nutrition as Preventive Medicine: Evaluating the Impact of Dietary Quality and Timing on Cardiometabolic Outcomes
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

ai.headline: Better diet quality and meal timing may lower heart and metabolic disease risk.
ai.summary: This narrative review looked at eighteen studies on dietary patterns and cardiometabolic health in adults. It found plant-forward diets such as Mediterranean and DASH were linked to lower risks of heart events, better blood pressure and lipids, while time-restricted eating was linked to modest weight loss and better blood sugar control. Higher ultra-processed food intake was linked to higher coronary disease risk.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that everyday food choices and when you eat them are linked to long-term heart and metabolic health.
ai.life_skill: Try choosing more whole, plant-based foods and fewer ultra-processed items.
ai.fact: Higher consumption of ultra-processed foods was linked with up to 19% higher coronary disease risk.

quiz.question: Which dietary patterns were linked to lower cardiometabolic risk in the review?
quiz.answer: Plant-forward dietary patterns such as Mediterranean and DASH diets were linked to lower cardiometabolic risk.

ai.caveat: The review is narrative and most evidence is observational, so it cannot prove that diet changes cause better health outcomes.

items.title: Effectiveness of Conversational Agents for Depression and Anxiety: Systematic Review and Network Dose-Response Meta-Analysis of Agent Types, Dose, and Human Support.

ai.headline: Chatbots with human support may help depression and anxiety, but evidence is very weak.
ai.summary: Researchers reviewed 41 randomised trials involving 7,577 people comparing different types of conversational agents for depression and anxiety. AI-enhanced intensive human support appeared to improve symptoms more than pure human digital guidance or open-ended multimodal chatbots, while most other comparisons were not significant. The overall certainty of evidence was very low due to risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that digital mental-health tools are promising but not yet proven enough to rely on without more high-quality research.
ai.life_skill: Try using a reputable mental-health app as extra support, but speak to a qualified professional if you feel low or anxious.
ai.fact: Conversational agents are digital tools that simulate conversation to deliver mental-health support.

quiz.question: What did the review conclude about the strength of the evidence for chatbots helping depression and anxiety?
quiz.answer: The overall certainty of evidence was very low, so confidence in the findings is limited.

ai.caveat: The evidence was rated very low certainty, with publication bias for depression and most comparisons not statistically significant.

items.title: Integrating GWAS meta-analysis with human brain cell mapping implicates the amygdala and cortical inhibitory interneurons in tinnitus

ai.headline: Tinnitus risk is linked to genes active in emotion-related brain cells, not just hearing pathways.
ai.summary: Researchers analysed genetic data from nearly one million adults across 19 cohorts to find variants linked to tinnitus. They found five significant genetic regions and evidence that tinnitus heritability concentrates in amygdala and cortical inhibitory neurons rather than the ascending auditory pathway.
ai.why_it_matters: It suggests tinnitus may involve brain systems beyond hearing, which could shape how researchers think about its causes and future support.
ai.life_skill: Notice that tinnitus may involve more than the ears, and discuss persistent ringing with a qualified health professional.
ai.fact: Tinnitus genetic risk is linked to cell types in the amygdala and cortical inhibitory interneurons rather than the ascending auditory relay.
ai.caveat: This is a preprint not yet peer reviewed, and the findings are based on genetic associations rather than proof of cause.

items.title: The effect of self-determination interventions on reading outcomes for middle and high school students with learning disabilities: A systematic review

ai.headline: Self-determination interventions may improve reading for secondary students with learning disabilities.
ai.summary: This systematic review looked at seventeen studies from 1982 to 2025 on self-determination interventions for middle and high school students with learning disabilities. It found that reading outcomes improved when these interventions were used.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows a practical, low-cost way schools might help teenagers with learning disabilities read better.
ai.life_skill: Try setting your own reading goals and checking your progress regularly.
ai.fact: Self-determination interventions are described as practical, low-cost, and easily implemented strategies for improving reading outcomes among secondary students with learning disabilities.

quiz.question: What did the review find about self-determination interventions and reading outcomes for middle and high school students with learning disabilities?
quiz.answer: Reading outcomes improved when self-determination interventions were used.

ai.caveat: The review included studies with varying designs and quality, so the results are not proof that the interventions caused the improvement.

items.title: A systematic review of emotional experiences of climate change and extreme weather events among children and adolescents: Implications for mental health and climate action
items.venue: The Journal of Climate Change and Health

ai.headline: Children and teens feel a range of emotions about climate change, which can cause distress or motivate action.
ai.summary: This systematic review analysed 30 studies on how children and adolescents emotionally respond to climate change and extreme weather. It found that media coverage, direct experiences, and feelings of agency shape these emotions, which can affect mental health and climate engagement. Supportive communication and involvement in action were linked to resilience and pro-environmental behaviour.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that climate-related feelings in young people are normal responses to a real issue and can be managed through validation and collective action.
ai.life_skill: Talk openly with trusted adults or peers about how climate change makes you feel and look for ways to take collective action.
ai.fact: Climate-related emotions such as eco-anxiety are described as valid responses to a real and ongoing crisis.

quiz.question: What did the review find about the effect of climate-related emotions on young people?
quiz.answer: Some emotions contribute to distress while others motivate constructive engagement with climate action.

ai.caveat: The review includes observational and qualitative studies, so it shows links between emotions and outcomes rather than proving cause and effect.

items.title: A frontier machine intelligence for human neuroimaging

ai.headline: An AI trained on nearly one million brain scans can interpret imaging and discuss findings like a radiologist.
ai.summary: Researchers developed Neuro-VL, a vision-language model trained on nearly one million neuroimaging studies from routine clinical care. It outperformed general-purpose and specialized medical models in diagnosing, localizing, and describing abnormalities, generating radiology reports, comparing serial scans, and resisting misleading assumptions.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how AI might one day help doctors interpret brain scans faster and more consistently, potentially improving diagnosis and monitoring of neurological conditions.

quiz.question: What kind of model is Neuro-VL?
quiz.answer: A vision-language model trained on nearly one million neuroimaging studies from routine clinical care.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint that has not yet been peer reviewed, so the findings are preliminary and not yet confirmed.

items.title: PRISM - Predictive Reasoning and Interactive Sequential Modeling for Disease Management

ai.headline: A computer model predicted future diagnoses from health records and explored how tests and treatments might change those predictions.
ai.summary: Researchers built PRISM, an AI framework using electronic health records from over 113,000 patients, to predict future diagnoses in inflammatory bowel disease. It correctly identified the exact next diagnosis about 15% of the time, rising to 49% within the top five guesses, and showed how masking certain biomarkers or adding medications changed predicted risks.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how AI might one day help doctors spot likely future health problems and test treatment ideas using routine records.
ai.fact: The model’s Top-10 accuracy reached 86.52% when any of the next ten diagnoses was accepted.

quiz.question: What did PRISM use to predict future diagnoses?
quiz.answer: It used structured longitudinal electronic health records from a large patient cohort.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint that has not been peer reviewed, and the findings are associations from a model rather than proof that the predictions or treatments work in real patients.

items.title: It Was Better Not to Know: Digital Recognition, Family Authority, and Postpartum Mental Health in Bangladesh

ai.headline: Mothers in Bangladesh found postpartum distress online but could not act without family approval.
ai.summary: Researchers interviewed 20 mothers in urban, slum and rural Bangladesh who had given birth in the past two years. Mothers learned about postpartum depression through Facebook and YouTube recommendations and used these platforms to make sense of their feelings privately, but families often dismissed their distress, leaving them with knowledge but no authority to seek help.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that recognising a mental-health problem online is not enough when family members control whether support is sought.
ai.life_skill: Notice whether family members are open to talking about low mood after childbirth before expecting them to support you.
ai.fact: Postpartum mental distress affects roughly one in five mothers in low- and lower-middle-income countries.

quiz.question: How did mothers in the study first encounter the idea of postpartum depression?
quiz.answer: They came across it incidentally through Facebook and YouTube recommendations rather than by searching for it or receiving clinical guidance.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint based on interviews with only 20 mothers, so the findings are not yet peer reviewed and may not apply more widely.

items.title: Thought for food: Individual differences in how food decisions are made

ai.headline: Healthier food choices may come from seeing healthy foods as tasty, not just using self-control.
ai.summary: A large US sample of 1,052 people rated foods on 17 dimensions, which were reduced to three core attributes: tastiness, healthiness and umami. All three attributes influenced choices, and people who chose healthier foods tended to see those foods as tastier rather than relying only on self-control. Higher eating restraint was linked to less deliberation, suggesting more automatic decision-making.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that healthy eating can involve enjoying healthy food, not just resisting temptation, which may make lasting dietary change feel easier.
ai.life_skill: Notice whether you think of healthy foods as tasty, and try choosing ones you genuinely enjoy.
ai.fact: Tastiness, healthiness and umami all influenced food choices in this study.

quiz.question: What did people who made healthier food choices tend to believe about healthy foods?
quiz.answer: They perceived subjectively healthier foods as tastier.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint that has not yet been peer reviewed, and the cross-sectional design cannot show that one factor causes healthier choices.

items.title: RADx-UP- Impact of Community Health Worker Deployment

ai.headline: A trial tests whether community health workers can boost COVID-19 vaccine confidence and diabetes self-management in rural Georgia households.
ai.summary: The study will send community health workers to the homes of adults at higher risk from COVID-19 and diabetes, including those with uncontrolled diabetes or prediabetes who are unvaccinated. Health workers will provide education on diabetes and COVID-19 vaccines, take blood glucose measurements, and offer assessments to other adults in the household.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how trusted local workers might help underserved rural families manage long-term health and make informed vaccine choices.
ai.life_skill: Check whether trusted community health workers in your area offer free home visits or health checks for diabetes and vaccines.
ai.fact: Community health workers are being tested as a way to deliver diabetes education and COVID-19 vaccine information directly to people’s homes.

quiz.question: Who will the community health workers visit in this trial?
quiz.answer: Adults at increased risk from COVID-19 and diabetes, including people with uncontrolled diabetes or prediabetes who have not had a COVID-19 vaccine.

ai.caveat: This is a trial record describing a planned study, so results are not yet available and it cannot show whether the intervention worked.

items.title: More than exercise: health-related quality of life and participation motives in dragon boating among people with breast cancer—a cross-sectional study

ai.headline: Breast cancer survivors with lower wellbeing may join dragon boating to cope emotionally.
ai.summary: Researchers surveyed 156 German breast cancer survivors who take part in dragon boating about their quality of life and reasons for joining. Those with lower psychological wellbeing, physical functioning, and social functioning reported stronger motives to join for distraction and emotional release, while greater pain was linked to a stronger motive related to aesthetics.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how group sport can serve as a coping strategy for people managing breast cancer.
ai.life_skill: Notice whether you are drawn to an activity for emotional release or distraction, and consider what need it might be meeting.
ai.fact: Lower psychological wellbeing, physical functioning, and social functioning were associated with stronger distraction/catharsis motives among breast cancer survivors in dragon boating.

quiz.question: What was linked to stronger motives of distraction and emotional release in dragon boating among breast cancer survivors?
quiz.answer: Lower psychological wellbeing, physical functioning, and social functioning were associated with stronger distraction/catharsis motives.

ai.caveat: This was a cross-sectional observational study, so it cannot show that dragon boating caused changes in wellbeing or coping.

items.title: Heat-induced increases in xylem vulnerability: Experimental evidence and possible mechanisms

ai.headline: Heat can make trees more vulnerable to drought by weakening their water-carrying tissue.
ai.summary: Researchers tested seven Australian and European tree species and found that exposure to higher temperatures reduced resistance to embolism and sped up drying, though the effect varied by species and was clearest in Australian trees.
ai.why_it_matters: It helps explain why hotter droughts may kill more trees than expected from water shortage alone.
ai.fact: Heat exposure can reduce embolism resistance in tree xylem, meaning water transport fails at less negative water potentials.

quiz.question: What did heat exposure do to embolism resistance in the tested trees?
quiz.answer: It reduced embolism resistance, on average at 0.73 MPa less negative water potentials.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint not yet peer reviewed, and the clear effects were found only in Australian species.

items.title: Ocean absorbs more fossil fuel carbon while land uptake stalls, 30 years of data show

ai.headline: The ocean is absorbing more fossil-fuel carbon, while land carbon uptake has stalled since 1990.
ai.summary: Researchers analysed 30 years of data on carbon dioxide from fossil fuels. They found the ocean’s absorption of this carbon has increased since 1990, while forests, soils and other land ecosystems have not increased their net uptake.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how the planet’s natural systems are responding differently to human carbon emissions, which affects future climate change.
ai.life_skill: Notice how different natural systems, such as oceans and forests, respond to pollution in different ways.
ai.fact: The ocean has absorbed more fossil-fuel carbon dioxide since 1990, while land ecosystems have not increased their net uptake.

quiz.question: What happened to land carbon uptake between 1990 and the present according to the study?
quiz.answer: The net uptake of carbon by forests, soils and other land ecosystems has not grown.

ai.caveat: This is a single observational study based on 30 years of data, so it shows a link rather than proving cause and effect.

items.title: Yale scientists reveal what really slows aging and what doesn't

ai.headline: Some drugs, diet and exercise may slow biological aging, but popular supplements do not seem to work.
ai.summary: Researchers analysed 51 studies looking at anti-aging treatments. They found certain prescription drugs, healthy diets and exercise were linked to measurable slowing of biological aging, while popular anti-aging supplements appeared largely ineffective.
ai.why_it_matters: It helps people decide where to focus their efforts if they want to support healthy aging.
ai.life_skill: Try focusing on a balanced diet and regular movement rather than relying on anti-aging supplements.
ai.fact: Biological aging can be measured and may be influenced by lifestyle and medication.

quiz.question: What did the analysis find about popular anti-aging supplements?
quiz.answer: They appeared largely ineffective at slowing biological aging.

ai.caveat: Whether these biological changes actually extend life remains uncertain.

items.title: Researchers trial AI coach for diabetes

ai.headline: An AI coach is being trialled to help people with type 2 diabetes stick to daily self-care.
ai.summary: The article describes a trial of an AI coach designed to support people with type 2 diabetes in consistently managing eating, exercise and medication. It notes that diabetes can progress quietly, so missed doses or skipped activity may not cause immediate warning signs.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how technology might help people turn health knowledge into everyday habits when the consequences of skipping care are not immediately obvious.
ai.life_skill: Try setting a simple daily reminder for your medication or a short walk so healthy intentions do not slip.
ai.fact: Type 2 diabetes management often depends on long-term consistency with eating, exercise and medication.

quiz.question: Why might people with type 2 diabetes find it hard to keep up healthy habits?
quiz.answer: Because diabetes can progress quietly, so missing a dose or skipping exercise may not cause immediate consequences.

ai.caveat: This is a news report about a trial, not the trial results themselves, so no findings are confirmed.

items.title: Kay Dickersin: pioneer of evidence based medicine and a founder of the Cochrane Collaboration

ai.headline: Trials with positive results are more likely to be published than those showing no effect or harm.
ai.summary: In 1987, researchers asked 318 authors of published randomised trials whether they had taken part in trials that were never published. Among completed but unpublished trials, 14% favoured the new treatment, compared with 55% of published trials. Most unpublished trials were simply never written up or submitted, usually because the results were negative or uninteresting.
ai.why_it_matters: If only trials showing benefit get published, reviews, guidelines and doctors may overestimate treatment benefits and underestimate harms.
ai.life_skill: Check whether health claims are based on all the available trial evidence, not just the published studies.
ai.fact: Published trials are more likely to report that a new treatment works than unpublished trials.

quiz.question: What did the 1987 study find about unpublished trials compared with published ones?
quiz.answer: Only 14% of unpublished trials favoured the new treatment, while 55% of published trials did.

ai.caveat: This is a single observational study based on authors’ reports, so it shows a link rather than proving causation.

items.title: The zoo of the gene networks capable of pattern formation by extracellular signaling

ai.headline: Mathematical rules limit how cells organize into body patterns to just three basic network types.
ai.summary: Researchers used mathematical proofs to analyse how gene networks allow cells to communicate and form patterns in the body. They found that despite many possible network structures, only three fundamental classes can actually create these patterns.
ai.why_it_matters: It reveals that the complex anatomy of living things follows simple, predictable mathematical rules rather than random chance.
ai.fact: All gene network topologies capable of pattern formation fall into only three fundamental classes and their combinations.

quiz.question: How many fundamental classes of gene networks can form body patterns?
quiz.answer: There are only three fundamental classes and their combinations.

ai.caveat: This is a theoretical mathematical model, so it describes logical possibilities rather than directly proving how every specific biological system operates in real time.

items.title: Scientists capture electrons making seemingly impossible quantum jumps

ai.headline: Scientists observed electrons jumping across forbidden energy gaps in graphene with 100% success in some cases.
ai.summary: Researchers studied electrons in graphene and captured them making quantum jumps across energy gaps that should be impossible. Some of these transitions happened with 100% probability. The finding gives a new view of quantum behavior and may lead to ultrafast, light-controlled electronics.
ai.why_it_matters: It deepens understanding of quantum physics and could one day lead to faster electronic devices.
ai.fact: Electrons in graphene can jump across forbidden energy gaps, with some transitions occurring at 100% probability.

quiz.question: What did scientists capture electrons doing in graphene?
quiz.answer: They captured electrons making jumps across forbidden energy gaps, with some transitions at 100% probability.

ai.caveat: This is a news report about a scientific finding, not the full peer-reviewed study, so details and independent verification are not provided.

items.title: [Correspondence] The Perth Declaration to eliminate rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease
authors: Jagat Narula, Garry Jennings, Derek P Chew

ai.headline: Rheumatic heart disease is linked to social inequity and mainly affects young people and women.
ai.summary: The authors highlight that rheumatic heart disease persists alongside deep social inequity. About 55 million people live with it and more than 370,000 die each year. It is the most common acquired heart disease in people under 25 and affects more women and girls than men and boys.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how social disadvantage can shape who benefits from medical progress and who dies young from this heart condition.
ai.fact: Rheumatic heart disease is the most common acquired heart disease in people younger than 25.

quiz.question: Which group is most affected by rheumatic heart disease?
quiz.answer: It is the most common acquired heart disease in people younger than 25 and affects more women and girls than men and boys.

ai.caveat: This is a correspondence piece, not a research study, so it does not provide new evidence or prove that inequity causes the disease.

items.title: Flood victim, 95, lived in Wetherspoons until she died after her home was destroyed

ai.headline: A 95-year-old flood victim lived in a pub until she died after her home was destroyed.
ai.summary: The report describes Jean Powell, aged 95, whose flat was flooded when the River Monnow burst its banks. She stayed in a Wetherspoons pub until she died, repeatedly asking when she could return home.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how flooding can displace older, vulnerable people and disrupt their lives long after the water recedes.
ai.fact: Flooding can make homes uninhabitable and force residents to live elsewhere for long periods.

quiz.question: What caused Jean Powell's flat to flood?
quiz.answer: The River Monnow burst its banks.

ai.caveat: This is a single news story about one person, not research, so it cannot show how common this experience is.

items.title: Noise pollution is reshaping the health and behaviour of animals everywhere

ai.headline: Human-made noise is nearly everywhere and affects animal health and behaviour.
ai.summary: The article reports that disruptive human noise reaches almost everywhere on Earth and is changing animal health and behaviour. It also describes noise pollution as one of the easier environmental problems to solve.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how everyday sound can affect wildlife and why reducing noise could be a practical way to help.
ai.life_skill: Try noticing where human-made noise is loudest around you.
ai.fact: Disruptive human noise reaches almost every part of the Earth.

quiz.question: According to the article, where is disruptive human noise found?
quiz.answer: There is almost nowhere on Earth free from it.

ai.caveat: This is a news report, not a research study, so it offers no specific data or proof of effects.

items.title: Effect of physical activity interventions on blood pressure control among adults with hypertension in Africa: a systematic review

ai.headline: Moderate-intensity exercise like brisk walking can lower blood pressure in adults with hypertension in Africa.
ai.summary: A systematic review of five studies examined physical activity programmes for adults with high blood pressure in Africa. Moderate-intensity aerobic exercise, especially brisk walking and aerobic dance, substantially reduced systolic blood pressure and had smaller favourable effects on diastolic blood pressure. Programmes lasting 12 to 16 weeks or longer, and those combined with medication, showed the strongest results.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that regular, moderate exercise can be a practical, low-cost part of managing high blood pressure alongside medical care.
ai.life_skill: Try adding regular brisk walking or aerobic dance to your routine if you have high blood pressure, but discuss it with a healthcare professional first.
ai.fact: Moderate-intensity aerobic exercise can lower systolic blood pressure in adults with hypertension.

quiz.question: Which types of exercise were found to substantially reduce systolic blood pressure?
quiz.answer: Moderate-intensity aerobic exercises, especially brisk walking and aerobic dance.

ai.caveat: The findings rest on only five studies, so they may not apply to all African settings or populations.

items.title: Efficacy of Digital Health Interventions for Insomnia: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.

ai.headline: Digital health interventions help insomnia
ai.summary: Researchers studied digital health interventions for insomnia, comparing them to controls in 44 trials. They found that these interventions improved sleep outcomes, including insomnia severity and sleep quality. However, the evidence was not strong enough to recommend them as a standard substitute for face-to-face therapy.
ai.why_it_matters: This matters because insomnia is a common problem and digital health interventions could provide a more accessible treatment option for some people.
ai.life_skill: Try exploring digital health interventions as a low-intensity option for managing insomnia, under the guidance of a healthcare professional.
ai.fact: Digital health interventions can improve sleep outcomes for people with insomnia.

quiz.question: What type of therapy is often used as a standard treatment for insomnia?
quiz.answer: Face-to-face cognitive behavioral therapy.

ai.caveat: The evidence was not strong enough to recommend digital health interventions as a standard substitute for face-to-face therapy, due to wide prediction intervals and moderate certainty.

items.title: Genetic architecture and polygenic prediction of self-reported response to selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors in individuals with depression: a genome-wide meta-analysis

ai.headline: Genes linked to antidepressant response
ai.summary: Researchers studied the genetic factors influencing response to antidepressants in individuals with depression. They found that certain genetic variants, particularly those related to neurotransmission, were associated with self-reported response to selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. The study also identified a link between genetic loading for psychiatric conditions and poorer response to antidepressants.
ai.why_it_matters: Understanding the genetic factors influencing antidepressant response can help improve treatment outcomes for individuals with depression
ai.life_skill: Consult a doctor before starting or changing antidepressant medication
ai.fact: Genetic variants related to neurotransmission are linked to antidepressant response

quiz.question: What type of neurotransmission was implicated in the study?
quiz.answer: GABAergic and glutamatergic neurotransmission

ai.caveat: This is a preprint study that has not yet been peer reviewed, so the findings should be interpreted with caution

items.title: Lower symptom burden strengthens the association between DTI-ALPS index and brain aging in head and neck cancer survivors

ai.headline: Cancer survivors show accelerated brain aging
ai.summary: Researchers studied brain aging in head and neck cancer survivors using diffusion MRI and symptom burden data. They found that survivors showed accelerated brain aging, with alterations in limbic white matter pathways. The study also found that higher DTI-ALPS index values were associated with reduced brain aging, particularly in survivors with lower symptom burden.
ai.why_it_matters: This study highlights the importance of brain health in cancer survivorship and its potential impact on everyday life
ai.life_skill: Try to manage your symptoms to potentially reduce brain aging
ai.fact: Head and neck cancer survivors can experience accelerated brain aging

quiz.question: What was found to be associated with reduced brain aging in cancer survivors?
quiz.answer: Higher DTI-ALPS index values were associated with reduced brain aging

ai.caveat: The study's findings are based on a single observational study and may not be causal or generalizable to all cancer survivors

items.title: Self-guided web-based mindfulness and skills-based distress reduction training versus treatment as usual optimised in patients with cancer (Reduct): a multicentre, parallel-group, randomised controlled trial

ai.headline: Mindfulness helps with cancer distress
ai.summary: Researchers studied the effect of a self-guided web-based mindfulness intervention on cancer patients' distress. The intervention was compared to optimised treatment as usual. Both groups showed improvement in distress, but the intervention group had significant improvements in anxiety symptoms and self-efficacy.
ai.why_it_matters: This study matters because it suggests that electronic mental health interventions can be a useful addition to traditional cancer care, providing patients with accessible support for their mental health.
ai.life_skill: Try exploring online mindfulness resources to help manage stress and anxiety.
ai.fact: Electronic mental health interventions can provide low-threshold psychosocial support for cancer patients.

quiz.question: What type of intervention was studied in this trial?
quiz.answer: A self-guided web-based mindfulness intervention.

ai.caveat: The study found no significant difference in overall distress between the intervention and control groups, which may limit the conclusions that can be drawn.

items.title: Experience-Handoff Reinforcement Learning for Recursive Self-Improvement

ai.headline: AI agents can improve by learning to write useful notes for their future selves.
ai.summary: Researchers tested a method where an AI agent not only performs tasks but also learns to create and curate 'playbooks' or notes from its past experiences. By training the AI to evaluate how well these notes help it in future tasks, the system achieved better performance on agentic benchmarks than methods that only focus on immediate actions.
ai.why_it_matters: It suggests that for both humans and AI, the way we record and refine our past lessons is as important as the actions we take in the moment.
ai.life_skill: When learning a new skill, try writing down specific 'playbooks' or checklists after each attempt to see if they help you next time.
ai.fact: Training AI agents to optimize the notes they pass to future versions of themselves can lead to better long-term performance.

quiz.question: What specific part of the AI's process did the researchers train to improve future performance?
quiz.answer: They trained the model to curate and evaluate the 'playbooks' or experience notes it hands off to future rollouts.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint not yet peer-reviewed, and the results are based on specific AI benchmarks rather than real-world human applications.

items.title: Integrating genre-based writing pedagogy and systematic instructional design to foster learner autonomy in Arabic academic writing: a mixed-methods study in Indonesian universities

ai.headline: A structured writing course helped Indonesian students improve their academic Arabic writing skills.
ai.summary: Researchers developed a teaching model combining genre-based writing with systematic design to boost learner autonomy. In a trial with 53 students, those using the model showed a significant improvement in their academic writing scores compared to their pre-test results.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that writing skills are not just about talent but can be built through specific, supportive teaching methods that encourage independent learning.
ai.life_skill: Notice how structured feedback and clear steps can help you improve a complex skill like writing.
ai.fact: Academic writing habits do not develop spontaneously and require both internal drive and a supportive instructional environment.

quiz.question: What was the main goal of the learning model developed in this study?
quiz.answer: The model aimed to foster learner autonomy in Arabic academic writing by focusing on paragraph-level competencies.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint that has not yet been peer reviewed, and the study used a quasi-experimental design with a small sample size.

items.title: Primer: An AI Framework for Instructor-Centered Educational Simulation Creation

ai.headline: A new open-source tool helps teachers use AI to build custom practice simulations for students.
ai.summary: This preprint introduces Primer, an AI system that assists educators in creating adaptive educational simulations. It allows teachers to input their specific knowledge and goals, while the AI generates responsive practice scenarios to support learning.
ai.why_it_matters: It suggests a future where personalised, high-quality practice tools are easier for teachers to create, potentially making education more adaptable to individual needs.
ai.life_skill: Notice how technology can support, rather than replace, the expertise of human teachers in creating learning experiences.
ai.fact: Primer is designed to be 'LLM-agnostic', meaning it can work with various AI models, including local and open-source ones.

quiz.question: What is the main role of the educator in the Primer system?
quiz.answer: The educator contributes their subject knowledge, lesson goals, and understanding of students to guide the AI's output.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint describing a new software framework, not a peer-reviewed study proving that using it improves student learning outcomes.

items.title: Learning What Matters: Goal certainty shapes working memory prioritization

ai.headline: As people become more certain about a rule, they remember only the relevant details and forget the rest.
ai.summary: Researchers tested 104 people on a task where a hidden rule changed without warning, requiring them to work out which feature mattered. As certainty about the rule grew, participants relied more on the relevant feature and their memory for irrelevant features declined, while the precision of what they remembered stayed about the same.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how the mind narrows focus once it has figured out what is important, helping us manage limited attention in everyday decisions.
ai.life_skill: Notice when you feel sure about what matters in a task, and let yourself ignore the rest.
ai.fact: Working memory prioritisation shifts from broad to selective maintenance as rule certainty increases.

quiz.question: What happened to memory for irrelevant features as certainty about the rule increased?
quiz.answer: Memory for inactive features declined.

ai.caveat: This is a single preprint that has not yet been peer reviewed, so the findings are not yet established.

items.title: Changes in specific dimensions of English writing anxiety during AI chatbot-supported blended instruction: evidence from Chinese vocational college students

ai.headline: AI chatbot-supported English writing lessons reduced some writing anxiety in vocational students
ai.summary: A study of 120 Chinese vocational college students compared blended English writing instruction using an AI chatbot with conventional instruction over eight weeks.
